To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a fluorescent benzesulfonamide (1) has been found to bind to CA II and CA IX with similar modes, but with a roughly 2-fold higher affinity for the tumor-associated isoforms IX over II, and that this difference in binding affinity may account for its preferential targeting of CA IX in vivo.

the X-ray crystal structure and the molecular modeling study of 1 in complex with hCA II and hCA IX, respectively, have shown the binding mode and the interactions that the compound establishes in the two enzymes, and have provided the rationale for its selectivity toward hCA IX.

(1) the compound 1, a fluorescent sulfonamide, has a high affinity for hCA II and hCA IX and is a good imaging tool for tumors, (2) its binding to hCA IX is stronger than to hCA II because of a strong hydrogen bond formed by the carbonyl of the fluoresceen tail with the Arg130 residue, and (3) the X-ray structure of the adduct with hCA II is the basis for a successful molecular modeling study
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular recognition of a fluorescent antiproliferative sulfonamide by hCA II and IX.
the design and synthesis of new fluorescent sulfonamides that may be useful for the imaging of CA IX-expressing tumors.
the development of new fluorescent sulfonamides as CA IX inhibitors for tumor imaging, and with the design of novel CA IX inhibitors for the selective inhibition of this tumor-associated isoform.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the fluorescein moi-ety of 1 does not participate in any direct interactions with the enzyme active sites, but it strongly interacts with the protein surface, thus increasing the affinity for the tumor-associated hCA IX over the ubiquitous isoform hCAII.

the fluorescein moi- ety of the inhibitor does not participate in the binding to the CA active site, but its tail, containing a carboxylic group, does, and this is responsible for the higher affinity for CA IX over CA II.

the fluorescein moi-ety of 1 does not participate in any specific interaction within the active site of the enzyme, but it is involved in a number of van der Waals interactions with the protein, and it is responsible for the overall hydrophobic character of the compound.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the X-ray crystallographic and molecular modeling studies have allowed us to understand the molecular basis for the selective binding and inhibition of CA IX by the compound 1, and to rationalize its selectivity toward this isoform.
the X-ray crystallographic study of 1-hCA II complex has been instrumental to rationalize its binding mode to CA IX, and to explain why the compound selectively accumulates in hypoxic tumors.

the compound 1 is a useful fluorescent probe for CA IX and that its binding mode can be exploited to design new CA inhibitors that can be used for imaging hypoxic tumors and also for developing new antitumor drugs.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the fluorescein moiity is a good scaffold to design CA inhibitors with a tumor selectivity, since it can be modified in order to interact specifically with the amino acids present at the active site of the isoforms of interest.

the fluorescein scaffold of this compound is not essential for its binding to CAs and that it can be easily replaced by other scaffolds, which may result in more potent CA inhibitors, useful as imaging and/or therapeutic tools.
the fluorescein moi-ety of 1, besides its intrinsic fluorescence, is also a very good probe for the active site of CAs, and it can be easily modified for obtaining more potent CA inhibitors.
